video_title: The Bond Market Is Flashing a Major Warning | Steve Hanke
gist: Johns Hopkins economist Steve Hanke argues broad money (Divisia M4) growing 6.7% a year has already let the inflation genie out of the bottle, and that bond vigilantes are now repricing that plus Trump's tariffs, the US-Israeli war on Iran and a widening fiscal deficit into higher yields. He says markets remain complacent about a stock bubble that higher rates typically pop, expects another oil price spike once drawn-down inventories run out, dismisses gold revaluation as a meaningless bookkeeping entry, and pitches an Article V limited constitutional convention with a Swiss-style debt brake as the only real fiscal fix.

themes.theme: Bond vigilantes and the money-supply inflation impulse

insights.claim: Broad money measured by Divisia M4 (Center for Financial Stability) is growing at 6.7% per year, above the roughly 5-6% pace Steve Hanke says is consistent with a 2% inflation target, which he reads as inflation already being structurally embedded.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: A monetarist gauge running above target-consistent growth argues against betting on a fast return to 2% inflation and favors staying short duration in bonds.
insights.quote: the divvisia M4 measure which you can get it from the center for financial stability which is the I think the best measure and the broadest measure is growing at 6.7% per year

insights.claim: Steve Hanke says bond vigilantes have come out of hibernation and that the recent jump in US yields reflects three specific drivers: entrenched inflation from money growth, Trump's tariffs, and the US-Israeli war on Iran.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: It frames the yield move as a multi-factor repricing rather than a data blip, so each of the three drivers should be tracked as a separate rates risk.
insights.quote: the bond vigilantes seem to have come out of hibernation and and bond yields have have gone up significantly in just the past week

insights.claim: Hanke's operating framework is that significant changes in the money supply move nominal GDP with a lag, where nominal GDP equals real growth plus inflation, and broad money has been rising steadily for about the last 18 months.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Gives a lead indicator for inflation and nominal growth surprises that most rate forecasts ignore, useful for positioning ahead of CPI prints.

insights.claim: US mortgage rates are, per Hanke, as high as they have been since before the 2008 global financial crisis, and the housing market is flat and doing nothing, because everything is geared off the 10-year Treasury yield.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Housing-linked equities, mortgage REITs and homebuilders stay pressured as long as the 10-year keeps grinding higher.
insights.quote: mortgage rates are as high as they've been since since before the great financial crisis in 2008 and and the housing market is is by the way quite flat

insights.claim: Rising yields hit risk assets through two channels at once: bond prices fall as yields rise, and a higher discount rate mechanically lowers the present value of future free cash flows, which Hanke calls the background threat that eventually pops or deflates bubbles.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Long-duration equities and any asset priced off low discount rates carry the most downside if the vigilantes keep pushing yields up.
insights.quote: if the discount rate goes up what goes down down the present value

themes.theme: Oil inventory drawdown turning deficit into shortage

insights.claim: The muted oil price response to the Iran conflict is explained by inventory drawdowns substituting for reduced wellhead flows, a cushioning effect that hides the underlying supply deficit rather than eliminating it.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Current calm oil prices are not evidence the risk passed; watch inventory levels, not spot price, as the real early-warning gauge.

insights.claim: The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is down to its lowest level since 1983 and private inventories have also been run down, leaving little buffer against further Persian Gulf and Red Sea supply disruption.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: A depleted SPR removes the policy tool that has repeatedly capped oil spikes, raising the tail risk in energy prices and headline inflation.
insights.quote: if you take the strategic petroleum reserve in the United States it's down to the lowest level it's been since 1983

insights.claim: Steve Hanke predicts another spike in the oil price once inventories are drawn down to very low levels, if the war continues or the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea routes stay blocked.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Argues for owning energy or oil-linked optionality as a hedge, since the spike is delayed rather than avoided.
insights.quote: we eventually will get those inventories down at very low levels and I think we'll end up seeing another spike in the price of oil

insights.claim: Hanke distinguishes a deficit, which inventories can accommodate, from a shortage, which appears when inventories run out and can only be rationed by a price increase that forces demand destruction.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Sets a clear trigger to watch: the moment inventory cover stops rising to meet the shortfall, price rather than volume becomes the adjustment mechanism.
insights.quote: once you run out of inventory, you you don't no longer have a deficit. You have a shortage.

themes.theme: Hanke's eight-point verdict that the US lost the Iran war

insights.claim: Steve Hanke argues the US has already lost the war on Iran, citing eight unmet conditions: no regime change, unresolved nuclear enrichment, intact long-range ballistic missiles, continued Iranian support for Hezbollah, the Houthis and Hamas, a closed Strait of Hormuz, heavily damaged Gulf bases with US troops retreating into Jordan, frayed Gulf alliances, and China, Russia and Turkey as the winners.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: If the conflict is unwinnable rather than nearly over, geopolitical risk premia in oil, defense and Treasuries persist far longer than the market's usual look-through assumes.
insights.quote: China and Russia and Turkey have been the big winners out of the Gulf War

insights.claim: Hanke insists the causality on the Strait of Hormuz is reversed in popular commentary: the Strait had free passage before the war, the US initiated the closure by attacking Iran, and Iran only then shut it.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: If the closure is a response to US escalation, de-escalation rather than more force is the reopening catalyst traders should watch for shipping and oil.
insights.quote: The the Iranians didn't close it. The US did.

insights.claim: Hanke relays a report that Saudi Arabia's crown prince threatened to start dumping Treasury bonds if Trump proceeded with strikes on Iranian power plants and domestic infrastructure, and that this is a plausible reason the strikes were called off over the weekend.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Treasury holdings being used as an explicit foreign-policy lever means an escalation headline could translate directly into a yield spike via a bandwagon of official sellers.
insights.quote: if if you go ahead with this, we're going to start dumping Treasury bonds.

insights.claim: Hanke estimates the real accounting cost of the Iran war will end up around one trillion dollars, with the Secretary of War repeatedly going to Capitol Hill for another hundred billion at a time.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: War financing on that scale feeds directly into deficit-driven Treasury supply and therefore into the term premium.
insights.quote: the the real cost uh accounting cost will end up being probably around a trillion dollar

themes.theme: Complacent markets, widening deficit, and a bubble waiting on rates

insights.claim: Hanke's central market view is that equity and oil markets remain complacent and have not priced a long laundry list of risks, while the bond market is the one market now actually pricing them in.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Signals a cross-asset divergence trade: trust rates as the risk signal and treat equity calm as the lagging, mispriced side.
insights.quote: the the markets seem to be quite complacent about all these risk. We can go through a long laundry list of risk and they don't seem to be priced in

insights.claim: Hanke says every measure of bubbles flags the stock market as a bubble, that timing a pop is virtually impossible, and that the one reliable exception is higher interest rates, which historically accompany bubbles popping.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Gives an actionable trigger rather than a vague warning: use rising long yields as the tripwire for cutting equity risk.
insights.quote: we know the stock market's in a bubble. Any measure of bubbles, throw the thing up as a bubble.

insights.claim: Hanke adds an overarching fourth yield driver beyond inflation, tariffs and war: an out-of-control US fiscal deficit that forces more Treasury issuance, prompting buyers to demand a higher interest rate as risk compensation, with tariff revenue having failed to balance the budget as promised.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Supply-and-risk-premium dynamics argue for steeper curves and persistent pressure at the long end regardless of Fed policy.

insights.claim: Hanke warns investors not to assume markets can keep looking through geopolitical shocks, advising against taking an August vacation and ignoring markets.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Flags thin summer liquidity plus live escalation risk as a gap-risk setup worth hedging rather than sitting through.
insights.quote: don't take your August vacation and and, you know, not look at the markets.

themes.theme: China holds the cards while US industrial policy expands

insights.claim: China's economy is in the doldrums because its money supply is growing too slowly to hit its implicit 7% nominal GDP target, composed of a 5% real GDP target plus a 2% inflation target, and Hanke says it will not hit that target.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Bearish for China-linked cyclical demand and commodities absent a decisive monetary expansion, which itself would be the signal to reverse the view.
insights.quote: The the real GDP target is 5%. So So they actually have a nominal GDP target. It's 7%. 2% inflation 5% real.

insights.claim: Hanke sees a huge geopolitical shift away from the United States toward China, with international perception indices showing China moving from negative to positive and the US from positive to negative.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Supports a structural de-dollarization and reserve-diversification narrative that pressures Treasury demand and favors non-US assets.

insights.claim: Hanke argues China holds all the cards in the trade fight because it controls critical materials that, if squeezed or cut off, would throw a monkey wrench into both the US and European economies, leaving Washington without real tariff leverage.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Points to supply-chain chokepoint exposure in industrials, autos and semis, and to critical-minerals suppliers as the hedge.
insights.quote: China China does have all the cards because China can controls all the critical materials

insights.claim: Hanke says the anti-China posture is fully bipartisan, with Biden owning the sanctions architecture and Trump adding tariffs on top, so an administration change would not reverse the damage to US international standing.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Removes the election as a mean-reversion catalyst; investors should treat trade fragmentation as a persistent regime, not a policy cycle.
insights.quote: The the idea that somehow the Democrats are a lot different than the Republicans is a joke.

insights.claim: Hanke welcomes the absence of US tariff leverage and argues tariffs should be zero, framing tariffs and sanctions as weapons of economic warfare that convert trading partners into enemies, and citing roughly 80-85% of Canadians disliking Trump as evidence of the reputational cost.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: A view that tariff escalation is self-defeating implies eventual policy reversal risk for tariff-protected domestic producers.
insights.quote: I think it's wonderful that we don't have any leverage. I think they should be zero.

insights.claim: Hanke says the US government has taken equity stakes in 30 companies under Trump, which he calls a continuation of the industrial policy laid down under Biden and a path toward socialism regardless of party labels.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: State equity participation changes the risk profile of favored sectors, creating both subsidy upside and political-interference risk for holders.
insights.quote: this is this is down the path to socialism

themes.theme: Gold revaluation debunked as a bookkeeping entry

insights.claim: Hanke dismisses the idea that the US government repricing its gold would help the fiscal position, calling it irrelevant and just a bookkeeping entry that would change the books but nothing real, though it would excite gold bugs.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Fades a recurring gold-bull catalyst narrative; any rally on revaluation headlines would be sentiment, not a change in fiscal reality.
insights.quote: It's irrelevant, though. It's just a bookkeeping entry.

insights.claim: US gold is carried at a statutory $42.22 per ounce set by New Deal-era legislation and dating in its current form to 1973, and Hanke stresses the Treasury owns the gold while the Fed only holds gold certificates.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Clarifies the legal plumbing behind revaluation chatter, showing the Fed is not the owner and cannot capture the mark-to-market gain.

insights.claim: Hanke explains that only an actual sale of gold at the prevailing market price, not an accounting revaluation, could finance the current deficit, with the Fed receiving $42.22 per ounce and the residual flowing into the Treasury General Account at the Fed.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Sets the real test for any gold-monetization scheme: watch for actual sales into the market, which would be bearish gold, not balance-sheet marks.
insights.quote: the gold was sold the Fed would only get 4222 per ounce

themes.theme: Article V debt brake as the only fiscal exit

insights.claim: Hanke argues the only genuine way out of the US debt burden is invoking Article V of the Constitution for a limited constitutional convention that writes a debt brake into the Constitution, and he sits on the board of the Federal Fiscal Sustainability Foundation pushing exactly that.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Implies no near-term fiscal consolidation without a constitutional change, so the deficit-driven yield pressure has no policy off-ramp on current trajectory.

insights.claim: Hanke says enough states have already applied to trigger a constitutional convention under the two-thirds threshold, but Congress has stonewalled and refused to call it, and roughly half the applying states have specified a limited convention.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: A live but stalled process worth monitoring: an actual convention call would be a major, unpriced US fiscal-policy regime event.
insights.quote: right now we we actually have uh enough states have applied for the uh to invoke the convention that it they the Congress has stonewalled the thing.

insights.claim: Hanke points to the Swiss debt brake as the working model: the budget must balance over the business cycle and government spending growth cannot exceed economic growth, which caps government as a share of the economy and coincides with strong Swiss inflation, growth and productivity outcomes.
insights.speaker: Steve Hanke
insights.so_what: Offers a concrete benchmark for judging any proposed US fiscal rule, and supports the case that spending restraint need not kill growth.
insights.quote: the growth rate in government spending can't exceed the growth rate in the economy
